questions.stem: State the three sign patterns that make delta S total positive.
questions.modelAnswer: Both positive; surroundings positive and greater than a negative system term; system positive and greater than a negative surroundings term.

questions.stem: State the Gibbs equation with units for each term.
questions.modelAnswer: Delta G = delta H - T delta S, in kJ mol^-1, with T in K and delta S converted to kJ K^-1 mol^-1.

questions.stem: Explain how the Gibbs equation combines the two driving forces.
questions.modelAnswer: Delta H measures the enthalpy driving force and T delta S measures the entropy driving force on the same energy scale; subtracting them leaves the net driver, and its sign is the feasibility verdict.

questions.stem: A reaction has delta H = -100 kJ mol^-1 and delta S system = -100 J K^-1 mol^-1 at 500 K. Compute delta G.
questions.modelAnswer: Delta S becomes -0.100 kJ K^-1 mol^-1, so delta G = -100 - 500 x (-0.100) = -100 + 50 = -50 kJ mol^-1, still feasible at 500 K.

questions.stem: State the feasibility of exothermic reactions with positive delta S system.
questions.modelAnswer: Always feasible, at any temperature, since both terms are negative.

questions.stem: State the feasibility of endothermic reactions with negative delta S system.
Explain why heating enables endothermic, positive-entropy reactions.
questions.modelAnswer: The Gibbs term subtracts T delta S, so a positive entropy change converts rising temperature into an ever larger subtraction; past the flip point the subtraction covers the positive delta H and delta G turns negative.

questions.stem: An extraction is endothermic with positive delta S and fails at 298 K. Name the practical remedy.
questions.modelAnswer: Run it hot: furnace temperatures raise T delta S until delta G turns negative, which is exactly the blast-furnace remedy.

questions.stem: State the flip temperature for the aluminium oxide with carbon case.
Explain why the flip temperature marks feasibility's turning point.
questions.modelAnswer: At delta G = 0 the enthalpy price exactly equals the temperature-scaled entropy refund; below it delta G is positive for this class, above it negative, so the crossing temperature is the verdict boundary.

questions.stem: A change has delta H = +80 kJ mol^-1 and delta S = +200 J K^-1 mol^-1. Compute its flip temperature.
questions.modelAnswer: Delta S is 0.200 kJ K^-1 mol^-1, so T = 80/0.200 = 400 K; the change is feasible above 400 K.

questions.stem: State the two independent questions about any reaction.
questions.modelAnswer: Whether it is feasible (thermodynamic, delta G) and how fast it is (kinetic, Ea).

questions.stem: State the kinetic status of methane at room temperature in oxygen.
questions.modelAnswer: Kinetically stable - a high activation energy keeps it from reacting until ignited.

questions.stem: Explain why thermodynamic feasibility does not guarantee a visible reaction.
questions.modelAnswer: Delta G judges only the start and end states; a high activation barrier stands between them, so without ignition or a catalyst the mixture persists unchanged despite negative delta G.

questions.stem: A food company wants a feasible decomposition slowed at room temperature. Which lever do they pull, and why?
questions.modelAnswer: They pull the kinetic lever - lowering temperature or removing catalysts raises the effective barrier - because the thermodynamic feasibility cannot be changed without changing the chemistry.
